Question: A classifier plus a fixed email template is usually better than an agent when:
Option A: Every input maps to one of a few known actions
Option B: The next tool depends on unpredictable observations
Option C: You must browse and synthesize many unknown sources
Option D: The user goal cannot be enumerated

Question: A state machine (graph) agent differs from a free-form ReAct loop because:
Option A: Allowed transitions are explicit; the model cannot jump to an arbitrary tool at any time
Option B: State machines cannot call tools
Option C: Free-form loops cannot observe tool output
Option D: Graphs forbid timeouts

Question: A tool returns 500. The agent should not:
Option A: Retry with backoff if the error looks transient and the tool is safe to retry
Option B: Blindly retry in a tight loop with the same side-effecting payload
Option C: Surface a bounded failure to the user after a retry budget
Option D: Record the error in the trace

Question: An LLM agent, at minimum, is:
Option A: A single classification head with no tools
Option B: A loop: the model chooses actions (often tool calls), observes results, and continues until it stops
Option C: A database trigger
Option D: A tokenizer with a larger vocabulary

Question: An agent can run `shell` as root on production. What is the actual risk?
Option A: Tool calls are sandboxed by default, so the prompt cannot cause harm.
Option B: Prompt injection or a bad plan can execute irreversible commands; tools are permissions, not suggestions.
Option C: LLMs cannot emit function calls, so the shell tool will never fire.
Option D: Root is required for observability, so this is best practice.

Question: Episodic memory, in agent design, usually means:
Option A: Records of past runs or conversations you may retrieve later
Option B: The weights of the base model
Option C: The tokenizer merge table
Option D: GPU scratch space

Question: For AI agents, a ReAct-style loop thinks, calls a tool, observes, repeats. Why do you still need a max-step budget?
Option A: Tokenizers crash after 12 steps.
Option B: Without a stop condition the loop can spin (retries, confusion, tool errors) and burn time/money.
Option C: Tools automatically halt after one call.
Option D: The model remembers all prior steps forever, so budgets are only for UX.

Question: For AI agents, a step budget or timeout exists so that:
Option A: The agent cannot loop until money, time, or tools are exhausted
Option B: Temperature stays at 1
Option C: Memory is encrypted
Option D: Retrieval is disabled

Question: For AI agents, an over-permissioned tool is dangerous because:
Option A: The model might call it with a hallucinated argument and actually take the action
Option B: Tools cannot have side effects
Option C: Permissions only affect logging
Option D: Agents cannot call tools more than once

Question: For AI agents, retrying a “create payment” tool on timeout is risky unless:
Option A: The tool is idempotent or you pass an idempotency key
Option B: You retry as fast as possible
Option C: You hide the error from traces
Option D: You raise temperature

Question: For AI agents, tool use requires a schema because:
Option A: The model must emit arguments the runtime can parse and validate before execution
Option B: Schemas disable JSON
Option C: Tools ignore types
Option D: Schemas replace authentication

Question: Giving an agent a raw shell tool as “just in case” is a problem because:
Option A: It can run commands you never intended, including destructive or data-exfiltrating ones
Option B: Shells cannot return text
Option C: Models cannot emit command strings
Option D: Timeouts become infinite automatically

Question: If you have no traces, an agent that “sometimes does the wrong tool” is hard to fix because:
Option A: You cannot see the arguments, observations, or which step diverged
Option B: Wrong tools never happen
Option C: Logs are illegal for agents
Option D: The loop has only one step by definition

Question: Traces for agents should record:
Option A: Only the final paragraph shown to the user
Option B: Each model step, tool name, arguments, results, and errors, with timings
Option C: Only GPU temperature
Option D: Only the system prompt, never tool I/O

Question: When is a tool-using agent a worse choice than a plain function call / workflow?
Option A: Whenever the task has more than one step.
Option B: When the steps are known, deterministic, and must not invent a plan (refunds, payroll, migrations).
Option C: When you have APIs; agents cannot call APIs.
Option D: Never; agents are always more accurate because they can retry.

Question: When should you usually not use an agent?
Option A: The task is a deterministic pipeline or one model call with a known schema
Option B: The user goal is unknown and may need several tools
Option C: You must branch on intermediate observations you cannot precompute
Option D: You need open-ended research with tool use

Question: Which is working memory for an agent, not a long-term store?
Option A: The current prompt: instructions, recent observations, and scratch notes in this run
Option B: A vector index of all past tickets across months
Option C: A policy wiki in RAG
Option D: A user profile database

Question: A pipeline writes 10 million 1 KB files to S3 per day. Besides storage bytes, what usually dominates cost and pain?
Option A: Request (PUT/LIST) charges and slow LIST/rename patterns; many tiny objects are a request-tax design.
Option B: S3 minimum object size is 128 MB, so 1 KB files are rejected.
Option C: ETag computation requires an EC2 instance per object.
Option D: Tiny files cannot be encrypted, so KMS becomes the bottleneck.

Question: In AWS / S3, SNS fan-out to multiple SQS queues is useful when:
Option A: You need exactly-once across all consumers without idempotency
Option B: Several independent workers should each see the event; each queue still delivers at-least-once
Option C: S3 becomes a relational store
Option D: Prefix hotspots go away

Question: In AWS / S3, SQS standard queues are at-least-once. Your consumer must:
Option A: Assume each message is processed exactly one time
Option B: Be idempotent; the same message can be delivered more than once
Option C: Use S3 listing as the lock
Option D: Disable checksums

Question: In AWS / S3, a PUT of a new object should include integrity protection by:
Option A: Memorizing a durability percentage
Option B: Sending a checksum and verifying it on read; copies plus checksums are the durability story
Option C: Using sequential prefixes
Option D: Storing only in one AZ in the app

Question: In AWS / S3, durability of an object is achieved by:
Option A: A published SLA number you should memorize as the design
Option B: Storing multiple copies and verifying checksums so bit rot and disk loss do not silently win
Option C: Keeping one copy in the client's browser
Option D: Using SQS as the disk

Question: In AWS / S3, listing a bucket with millions of keys as your 'index' is a bad database because:
Option A: List is transactional
Option B: List is paginated, costly, and not a query planner; you needed a real index or a manifest object
Option C: List returns at-most-once keys
Option D: List evicts objects

Question: In AWS / S3, millions of tiny files (few KB each) get expensive and slow mainly because:
Option A: S3 forbids small objects
Option B: You pay per request and listing/metadata work dominates; throughput is not 'one disk sequential read'
Option C: Checksums fail under 1MB
Option D: Prefixes cannot hold small keys

Question: In AWS / S3, old-style keys like 2024-01-01/log1, 2024-01-01/log2 created prefix hotspots because:
Option A: Dates are invalid key characters
Option B: Many clients hammered the same key prefix/partition at once instead of spreading request load
Option C: S3 cannot store dates
Option D: Checksums collide on dates

Question: In AWS / S3, visibility timeout on SQS exists so that:
Option A: Messages become source of truth in S3
Option B: Other consumers hide the message while one works; if you crash, it reappears (at-least-once)
Option C: Duplicates are impossible
Option D: Prefixes spread automatically

Question: In AWS / S3, why spread entropy in the key (or a hash prefix) for high QPS ingest?
Option A: To make listing impossible
Option B: To avoid concentrating request rate on one logical prefix as the workload scales
Option C: To disable checksums
Option D: To force at-most-once SQS

Question: Putting a database dump on S3 is backup. Using S3 as the live order table is wrong because:
Option A: S3 cannot store bytes
Option B: You lack cheap conditional updates, queries, and low-latency item access as a primary OLTP store
Option C: Checksums disable writes
Option D: Buckets cannot be private

Question: S3 is the wrong place to implement 'query users where lastLogin > X' because:
Option A: Objects cannot store JSON
Option B: It is an object store: get-by-key, not a query engine with secondary indexes and predicates
Option C: S3 deletes data after one day
Option D: Prefixes are strongly transactional

Question: S3 read-after-write for new objects is strongly consistent now. That still does not make S3 a database because:
Option A: Consistency was the only missing SQL feature
Option B: You still have no rich queries, joins, or cheap partial updates — only object I/O
Option C: Checksums became optional
Option D: Prefixes became transactions

Question: Small-file problem on S3 is often fixed by:
Option A: One object per database cell
Option B: Batching many logical records into larger objects (and maybe a real database for metadata)
Option C: Shorter prefixes only
Option D: Disabling checksums

Question: Updating a 'row' in S3 means:
Option A: A SQL UPDATE of one field
Option B: Replace the whole object (or write a new version); there is no in-place field update
Option C: A strongly consistent multi-object transaction by default
Option D: A Scan of the bucket

Question: Why is S3 a poor substitute for a database when you need atomic updates to a JSON blob 100 times a second?
Option A: S3 objects are immutable versions; concurrent writers last-write-win and you have no transactions or secondary indexes.
Option B: S3 cannot store JSON, only images.
Option C: S3 strongly consistent GET still serializes all writes through one global lock, so it is slower but correct.
Option D: S3 will automatically turn the object into DynamoDB after 100 writes.

Question: You put millions of objects under the prefix `logs/2026-09-05/` and request rates spike. What S3 behavior should you design for?
Option A: S3 has no prefix performance; only bucket name matters.
Option B: Very hot prefixes can be rate-limited until S3 scales the keyspace; spread keys (or wait for scaling) rather than hammer one timestamp prefix.
Option C: S3 will shard by file extension automatically.
Option D: You must enable Transfer Acceleration or all PUTs fail.

Question: A service inserts keys uniformly at random. Why does a classic B-tree usually pay more disk writes per insert than an LSM tree?
Option A: Each insert can dirty a leaf page (and maybe split), forcing an in-place random page write
Option B: B-trees rewrite the entire tree on every insert
Option C: LSM trees never fsync and therefore never write
Option D: B-trees store every key in two copies by design

Question: A workload is almost all point lookups and short range scans with in-place updates. Why is a B-tree usually the better default than an LSM tree?
Option A: B-trees never write more than one page, so they have zero write amplification.
Option B: A B-tree keeps keys ordered on pages you can update in place and scan sequentially; LSM pays compaction and extra reads across levels.
Option C: LSM trees cannot store secondary indexes.
Option D: B-trees do not need a WAL, which removes fsync from the picture.

Question: An LSM tree absorbs writes into a memtable and WAL, then flushes sorted runs. What problem is compaction solving?
Option A: It encrypts old runs so they can be deleted from the WAL.
Option B: It merges overlapping sorted runs so reads do not have to search an ever-growing number of files, and it reclaims space from obsolete keys.
Option C: It converts the LSM into a B-tree once the dataset fits in RAM.
Option D: It is only used to build secondary indexes; primary key reads skip it.

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, a bloom filter returns a false positive for a missing key. What is the user-visible effect?
Option A: The engine returns a wrong value
Option B: An extra index/data read of that SSTable that then correctly reports the key absent
Option C: On-disk data is corrupted
Option D: Compaction starts immediately

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, after a crash, how is a lost memtable reconstructed?
Option A: Replay the WAL to rebuild in-memory state
Option B: Scan every SSTable for the newest key
Option C: Rebuild it from bloom filters
Option D: It cannot be recovered; those writes are gone

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, on an LSM point lookup, what does a bloom filter actually tell you?
Option A: The exact file offset of the key
Option B: The key is definitely not in this SSTable, or it might be
Option C: Which compaction level owns the key
Option D: Whether the memtable is full

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, what does read amplification usually mean for an LSM point get?
Option A: Bytes written per user write
Option B: How many disk reads or files you may touch to serve one user read
Option C: The size of the WAL in bytes
Option D: How many replicas must answer

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, what happens when a memtable fills under normal LSM operation?
Option A: The process blocks until the next restart
Option B: It is frozen, flushed as an immutable SSTable, and a new memtable takes writes
Option C: All older SSTables are deleted immediately
Option D: The WAL is discarded before the flush finishes

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, what is the memtable + WAL pair actually buying you in an LSM store?
Option A: Faster range scans than reading SSTables
Option B: A durable crash-recovery log plus a sorted in-memory buffer so acknowledged writes survive a crash
Option C: A replacement for compaction
Option D: A way to skip bloom filters on point lookups

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, why does making flushed SSTables immutable matter for concurrency?
Option A: Old files can still be mutated in place
Option B: Readers can use a file lock-free while a new file is being written elsewhere
Option C: The WAL can be skipped
Option D: The memtable can grow without bound

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, why might a single LSM point lookup inspect several SSTables?
Option A: Keys are hashed into random files with no order
Option B: The newest version of a key can live in any of several files produced over time
Option C: Bloom filters require reading every file
Option D: The WAL must be scanned on every lookup

Question: What is compaction's main job in an LSM engine?
Option A: Increase write amplification for its own sake
Option B: Merge SSTables, drop obsolete versions and tombstones, and bound how many files a read must check
Option C: Turn the LSM tree into a B-tree
Option D: Disable the WAL after the first flush

Question: Why are LSM range scans of a key span often heavier than the same scan on a B-tree?
Option A: LSM trees cannot iterate keys in sorted order
Option B: You must merge iterators across the memtable and many overlapping SSTables
Option C: Range scans always replay the WAL
Option D: Bloom filters block sequential access

Question: Why can LSM ingest a flood of random keys faster than a B-tree of similar durable settings?
Option A: User writes append to WAL and memtable instead of randomly updating leaf pages
Option B: LSM engines never fsync
Option C: B-trees cannot store random keys
Option D: Compaction is free and instantaneous

Question: Why do B-trees typically win on short range scans of nearby keys?
Option A: Leaf pages keep keys in sorted on-disk order with little file overlap, often with sibling links
Option B: They never split pages
Option C: They attach a bloom filter to every leaf
Option D: They keep all data only in memory

Question: Why do LSM engines almost always put a Bloom filter in front of each SSTable?
Option A: To compress keys so SSTables fit in RAM.
Option B: To skip files that definitely do not contain a key, cutting read amplification on point lookups.
Option C: To make range scans O(1).
Option D: To replace the WAL for crash recovery.

Question: Write amplification in an LSM tree is dominated by which activity?
Option A: Bloom-filter false positives
Option B: Rewriting the same live data again during compaction
Option C: B-tree page splits
Option D: Replica count in the cluster

Question: In C++, `std::move` on a local then using it again — what is actually true?
Option A: move guarantees the object is empty and safe to read as 0.
Option B: The object is in a valid but unspecified state; using it without reassignment is a logic bug.
Option C: move copies if the type has a destructor.
Option D: move is a runtime memcpy of the bytes only.

Question: In C++, a `std::vector<bool>` is returned and you take a reference to an element. Why is this type a famous trap?
Option A: vector<bool> is a bit-packed proxy; references/pointers to elements are not real bool&.
Option B: bool cannot live in a vector.
Option C: vector<bool> is faster and always the right default.
Option D: It is the only vector that does not reallocate.

Question: In C++, when should you prefer `unique_ptr` over `shared_ptr`?
Option A: Always use shared_ptr; unique_ptr cannot be returned from functions.
Option B: When one owner is enough: unique_ptr is cheaper (no control block/atomics) and makes ownership obvious.
Option C: unique_ptr cannot hold arrays, so shared_ptr is required for buffers.
Option D: shared_ptr is always lock-free and therefore faster.

Question: In C++, why is RAII (owning a resource in an object whose destructor releases it) the default answer to leaks and lock-forget bugs?
Option A: Destructors run on every control-flow exit from the scope, including exceptions, so release is tied to lifetime.
Option B: The compiler inserts garbage collection for RAII types.
Option C: RAII disables exceptions, so you cannot forget a catch.
Option D: new/delete become undefined if any class has a destructor.

Question: In C++, why is `std::string_view` pointing at a temporary `std::string` a dangling-view bug?
Option A: string_view copies the characters, so it cannot dangle.
Option B: string_view does not own the buffer; when the temporary dies the view is invalid.
Option C: Temporaries live until the process exits.
Option D: string_view is illegal on temporaries and will not compile.

Question: In C++, you `new` an object and `delete` it in some return paths but not after an early `return` on error. What is the RAII alternative?
Option A: Wrap the pointer in unique_ptr so the destructor deletes on every exit path.
Option B: Add more comments on the delete.
Option C: Use a raw pointer and a finally keyword.
Option D: Disable exceptions so early returns cannot happen.

Question: In C++, you compile without `-Wall` and ignore a `return` missing on one path. What class of bug is that?
Option A: A style issue with defined behavior (returns 0).
Option B: Undefined behavior: falling off a non-void function.
Option C: The compiler inserts throw.
Option D: C++ requires all paths to return, so this cannot compile.

Question: In C++, you include a using-directive `using namespace std;` in a header. Why is that a problem?
Option A: std cannot be used in headers.
Option B: Every translation unit that includes it gets std dumped into the global namespace, causing name clashes.
Option C: It disables ADL.
Option D: Headers cannot have using-declarations of any kind.

Question: In C++, you store pointers to vector elements, then `push_back` until capacity grows. What happened?
Option A: Pointers remain valid because vector is contiguous.
Option B: Reallocation invalidates pointers/iterators into the old buffer (undefined behavior if you use them).
Option C: vector is a linked structure, so pointers always stay valid.
Option D: push_back is illegal while pointers exist; it will not compile.

Question: In Cassandra, LWTs (lightweight transactions / IF clauses) are expensive mainly because they…
Option A: Skip the commit log
Option B: Run a Paxos-style round of agreement instead of a regular quorum write
Option C: Store extra bloom filters
Option D: Disable compaction

Question: In Cassandra, RF=3 and you write with CL=ONE. A client then reads with CL=ONE from a different replica. What can happen?
Option A: The read is guaranteed to see the write because ONE always hits the leader.
Option B: The read may miss the write: ONE only waits for one replica, which might not be the one that stored the write yet.
Option C: Cassandra will block the read until all replicas have the write.
Option D: CL=ONE automatically upgrades to QUORUM for the next read.

Question: In Cassandra, if RF=3 and you choose CL=ALL, what availability tradeoff did you make?
Option A: You can tolerate one replica down
Option B: Any one replica down makes the request fail, in exchange for seeing all copies
Option C: Writes become local-only
Option D: Hints are no longer stored

Question: In Cassandra, replication factor (RF) vs consistency level (CL): which statement is accurate?
Option A: RF is how many replicas store a partition; CL is how many replicas must respond for this read or write
Option B: They are the same setting with two names
Option C: CL decides where data is stored; RF decides how many acknowledgements you wait for
Option D: RF only applies to reads; CL only applies to writes

Question: In Cassandra, the coordinator node in a write path is responsible for…
Option A: Storing the only copy of the data
Option B: Sending the mutation to the replica set and waiting for CL acknowledgements
Option C: Choosing a new partition key
Option D: Running repair before every write

Question: In Cassandra, what do clustering columns control?
Option A: Which datacenter gets the write
Option B: Sort order of rows within a partition on disk and in queries
Option C: The replication factor
Option D: Whether hinted handoff is enabled

Question: In Cassandra, what does repair (anti-entropy) try to fix?
Option A: Hot partitions by splitting tokens automatically
Option B: Replicas that have diverged because of missed writes, downtime, or missed hints
Option C: The need for a partition key
Option D: Tombstone creation

Question: In Cassandra, what is hinted handoff for?
Option A: Speeding up range scans
Option B: The coordinator stores a hint when a replica is down, then replays it when the replica returns
Option C: Choosing the partition key
Option D: Replacing anti-entropy repair entirely

Question: In Cassandra, why is a full-table scan (ALLOW FILTERING / unbounded partition scan) a junior anti-pattern?
Option A: Cassandra cannot read more than one row
Option B: Data is partitioned by token; a cluster-wide scan fans out and can overwhelm many nodes
Option C: QUORUM forbids scans
Option D: Tombstones cannot be read

Question: In Cassandra, why should a partition not grow without bound (wide partition)?
Option A: Clustering order breaks after a few rows
Option B: Compaction, repair, caching, and reads of that partition concentrate work on one token and huge SSTable pieces
Option C: RF becomes 1 automatically
Option D: QUORUM cannot count replicas for wide partitions

Question: In Cassandra, with RF=3, what does a QUORUM write mean?
Option A: All 3 replicas must acknowledge
Option B: At least 2 replicas must acknowledge (majority of RF)
Option C: Only the coordinator stores the write
Option D: Exactly 1 replica must acknowledge

Question: In Cassandra, you need to fetch a user's last 100 events in time order. How should that be modeled?
Option A: Partition key = event id, so every event is its own partition for even load.
Option B: Partition key = user id, clustering key = event time, so one partition holds an ordered slice you can range-read.
Option C: A single partition for the whole table named `events` so ORDER BY always works globally.
Option D: Store events in a Cassandra collection column and let CQL sort them at query time across nodes.

Question: In Cassandra, you write at CL=ONE and later read at CL=ONE. Why might you miss your own write?
Option A: Cassandra never reads your own writes
Option B: The read may hit a replica that has not received the write yet
Option C: ONE always waits for all replicas
Option D: Tombstones block all reads at ONE

Question: What does the partition key actually control in Cassandra?
Option A: The on-disk sort order of rows inside a partition
Option B: Which node(s) own the data: it hashes to a token and thus a replica set
Option C: The consistency level of the query
Option D: Whether a bloom filter is used

Question: What is a tombstone in Cassandra?
Option A: A backup of a deleted SSTable
Option B: A deletion marker that must be stored and compacted away later so old values do not resurrect
Option C: A hint stored on a coordinator
Option D: A repair session identifier

Question: Why can a hot partition ruin a Cassandra cluster even when total QPS looks modest?
Option A: One token/partition is owned by a small replica set, so those nodes take all the load for that key
Option B: Cassandra cannot store large partitions
Option C: QUORUM is disabled for hot keys
Option D: Bloom filters stop working on busy nodes

Question: Why is DELETE in Cassandra not the same as 'the row is gone now'?
Option A: Deletes are stored as tombstones and kept until gc_grace so repair does not resurrect the row.
Option B: Cassandra cannot delete; you can only TTL the whole table.
Option C: DELETE drops the SSTable file immediately, which is why deletes are fast.
Option D: Deletes require a QUORUM of all clusters worldwide.

Question: In data structures and algorithms, DFS vs BFS for 'does a path exist in a huge, deep, narrow maze if you are memory-constrained'?
Option A: DFS uses stack proportional to depth, which can be smaller than BFS's frontier in a wide graph — but it can also go infinitely deep without extra guards
Option B: BFS always uses less memory than DFS
Option C: They use identical memory on every graph
Option D: Only union-find can test connectivity

Question: In data structures and algorithms, a Bloom filter says 'this user id is not in the set.' What can you conclude?
Option A: It is definitely not in the set — Bloom filters have false positives, not false negatives (for a static membership filter)
Option B: It might still be in the set; negatives are probabilistic
Option C: You must re-hash with a tree to confirm negatives
Option D: The filter is corrupted whenever it says no

Question: In data structures and algorithms, a Bloom filter says 'yes, this email was seen.' You skip sending. Risk?
Option A: False positive — you may skip a never-seen email; if skips are costly, store a real set or a cache in front of source of truth
Option B: False negative — Bloom filters invent missing emails
Option C: Union-find will correct it on the next hop
Option D: LRU will convert the maybe into a no

Question: In data structures and algorithms, a Bloom filter says a user id is 'not present'. How should you treat that?
Option A: It might be a false negative; check the database anyway.
Option B: Trust it: Bloom filters have false positives, not false negatives (for the items actually inserted).
Option C: It is a cache, so 'not present' means 'evicted', not 'absent'.
Option D: Bloom filters only work for strings, not ids.

Question: In data structures and algorithms, an LRU cache is hit on every request for a hot key. What must the structure do in O(1) expected time?
Option A: Hash map to the node plus a recency list (or equivalent) so lookup, move-to-front, and eviction of the tail are cheap
Option B: Scan the whole array to find the oldest timestamp
Option C: Rebuild a heap from scratch on every hit
Option D: BFS the keyspace

Question: In data structures and algorithms, consistent hashing places both keys and nodes on a ring. A node dies. What should happen to its keys?
Option A: They move to the next node(s) on the ring (or to replicas), not to a random reshuffle of the whole keyspace
Option B: Every key is rehashed with % (N-1)
Option C: A Bloom filter deletes the node
Option D: LRU evicts all keys cluster-wide

Question: In data structures and algorithms, why do textbook linked-list queues often lose to a ring buffer of the same logical operations on real hardware?
Option A: Each node is a separate allocation; pointer chasing misses cache and TLB, while a contiguous buffer hits cache lines and prefetches
Option B: Linked lists have worse big-O for enqueue than arrays in the RAM model
Option C: CPUs cannot follow pointers at all
Option D: The kernel refuses to allocate list nodes

Question: In data structures and algorithms, why is a linked list usually the wrong 'insert in the middle is O(1)' answer on real hardware?
Option A: Pointer chasing destroys cache locality; an array/vector often wins even if Big-O looks worse.
Option B: Linked lists cannot insert in the middle.
Option C: The OS forbids heap-allocated nodes in user space.
Option D: CPUs execute linked-list code in O(n^2) regardless of length.

Question: In data structures and algorithms, you add a cache node and want existing keys to mostly stay put. Why not hash(key) % N?
Option A: Changing N remaps almost every key; consistent hashing (or Rendezvous) moves only a ~1/N fraction
Option B: Modulo is cryptographically unsafe, so caches reject it
Option C: % N cannot be computed for strings
Option D: Heaps cannot store the modulus

Question: In data structures and algorithms, you have n chat rooms and union operations 'merge these two rooms' plus 'are these users in the same room?' Which structure?
Option A: Union-find (disjoint-set) with path compression / union by rank
Option B: A max-heap of room ids
Option C: BFS from user 0 on every query
Option D: A Bloom filter of pairs

Question: In data structures and algorithms, you iterate a large array of structs vs a linked list of the same structs, summing one field. Why is the array usually much faster?
Option A: Sequential access prefetches; the list jumps to heap allocations that evict useful cache lines
Option B: Arrays have better big-O for a linear scan than lists
Option C: Linked lists cannot store structs
Option D: The compiler forbids summing list nodes

Question: In data structures and algorithms, you need 'get user by id' at huge QPS, ids are arbitrary strings, no range queries. Which shape fits the workload?
Option A: Hash table (average O(1) point lookup) — a tree adds comparison overhead you do not need, a heap is not a dictionary
Option B: Binary heap, because it always stores the minimum id on top
Option C: Linked list, because pointers are faster than arrays
Option D: DFS forest, because ids form a graph

Question: In data structures and algorithms, you need O(1) expected lookup by id and do not need ordered iteration. What is the default structure, and when does it bite you?
Option A: Balanced BST: lookups are O(1).
Option B: Hash table: great until a bad hash, huge load factor, or you need range queries / sorted order.

Option D: VACUUM FULL runs after every COMMIT

Question: In PostgreSQL, a long-running report transaction sits idle in the same database as a busy OLTP table. Why can autovacuum fail to reclaim dead tuples on that table even after many updates?
Option A: VACUUM cannot run while any other session holds a snapshot older than the dead tuples
Option B: PostgreSQL never vacuums a table that still has indexes
Option C: Dead tuples are only stored in WAL and never in heap pages
Option D: Idle transactions automatically freeze all XIDs so vacuum has nothing to do

Question: In PostgreSQL, a query plan shows Seq Scan on a 50-row lookup table that has a btree index on the filter column. When is the sequential scan often the better choice?
Option A: When most of the table will be visited anyway, random index I/O costs more than reading the heap once
Option B: When the index is unique, sequential scan is always preferred
Option C: When work_mem is large, indexes are ignored
Option D: When the column is NOT NULL, btree indexes cannot be used

Question: In PostgreSQL, after an UPDATE that does not change any indexed column, you still see a new heap tuple. What MVCC behavior explains this?
Option A: PostgreSQL always copies the whole row so readers of the old snapshot keep a consistent version
Option B: Indexes store full row copies, so the heap is rewritten only for uniqueness checks
Option C: MVCC reuses the same tuple slot in place and never creates a new version
Option D: Updates are logged only in WAL; the heap is never rewritten until CHECKPOINT

Question: In PostgreSQL, streaming replication with a hot standby is lagging. Which primary-side behavior most directly grows replica apply delay?
Option A: Long transactions on the primary that produce a large WAL burst the standby must replay in order
Option B: Autovacuum on the standby rewriting the primary heap
Option C: synchronous_commit = on on the standby only
Option D: Creating a btree index on a temp table on the primary

Question: In PostgreSQL, table bloat after heavy UPDATE/DELETE is high, but pg_stat_user_tables.n_dead_tup is low. What can still make the table large on disk?
Option A: Free space is fragmented inside pages that are not returned to the OS without a rewrite
Option B: Dead tuples live only in indexes, never in the heap
Option C: WAL files are counted as table size
Option D: TOAST is never vacuumed so it always grows

Question: In PostgreSQL, why must VACUUM (not just autovacuum on one table) eventually freeze tuples cluster-wide?
Option A: Transaction IDs wrap around; unfrozen tuples would look like they are in the future
Option B: WAL cannot be recycled until every tuple is frozen
Option C: Hot standbys cannot connect unless all tables are frozen
Option D: Indexes become invalid when XIDs exceed 2 million

Question: In PostgreSQL, you added a B-tree index on a boolean `is_deleted` column that is false for 99% of rows. Most queries filter `WHERE is_deleted = false`. What is the most likely result?
Option A: The index will usually beat a sequential scan because booleans are tiny.
Option B: The planner will often ignore the index: it still has to visit almost every row.
Option C: PostgreSQL will automatically convert the B-tree into a partial index.
Option D: Writes get faster because the index is smaller than the heap.

Question: In PostgreSQL, you partition a large events table by day. Which query pattern fails to benefit and may get worse?
Option A: Queries that filter on a non-partition key, forcing the planner to scan every partition
Option B: Queries that constrain the partition key to a single day
Option C: COPY into the current day's partition
Option D: DROP of an old partition instead of DELETE

Question: In PostgreSQL, you set synchronous_commit = off for a burst of non-critical inserts. What failure mode did you accept?
Option A: A crash can lose recent committed transactions even though clients already saw COMMIT succeed
Option B: Replicas will refuse to apply WAL until the master is restarted
Option C: VACUUM will skip the table until the next CHECKPOINT
Option D: Indexes become invalid because index WAL is not written

Question: Why does PostgreSQL write to WAL before applying the same change to the heap file?
Option A: WAL is a compressed copy of the heap used to speed up sequential scans.
Option B: So a crash can replay committed work; the heap can be rebuilt from a durable log of changes.
Option C: WAL is only for logical replication and is not used on a single node.
Option D: The heap is append-only, so WAL is how updates find the old row.

Question: Your app opens a new PostgreSQL connection for every HTTP request and closes it at the end. Under load the database CPU is fine but new requests stall. What is the usual bottleneck?
Option A: SQL parsing cannot be cached across connections, so every query is planned from scratch and fills disk.
Option B: Each connection is a backend process; process/memory overhead hits `max_connections` long before query CPU does.
Option C: PostgreSQL allows only one query at a time for the whole cluster.
Option D: TLS handshakes are stored in WAL, so connections wait on checkpoints.

Question: In Python, `is` vs `==` for strings that look identical: when is `is` the wrong check?
Option A: `is` compares values; `==` compares identity.
Option B: `is` is object identity. Interning makes some equal strings share identity, but it is not a value comparison you should rely on.
Option C: `==` is illegal on strings.
Option D: They are the same for all objects except floats.

Question: In Python, a function is defined as `def append(item, bucket=[]):`. Why do later callers see other callers' items?
Option A: Lists are passed by name, so all calls share a global `bucket` variable.
Option B: The default list is created once at function definition and reused; mutations accumulate.
Option C: Python copies defaults on each call, but `[]` is interned like small integers.
Option D: This only happens in debug mode; production isolates defaults per request.

Question: In Python, a generator expression is passed to a function that iterates it twice. Why is the second pass empty?
Option A: Generators are one-shot iterators; after exhaustion they yield nothing unless you recreate them.
Option B: CPython copies generators into a list automatically on first use.
Option C: Functions always rewind generators to the start.
Option D: Generator expressions are tuples in disguise.

Question: In Python, a loop of nested functions is created as `funcs = [lambda: i for i in range(5)]`. Why do they all return 4?
Option A: lambda cannot capture loop variables in CPython.
Option B: Closures bind the variable, not the value at definition; they all read the final `i`.
Option C: range(5) is lazy and only evaluated when the lambda runs, always as 4.
Option D: list comprehensions run in reverse, so i is always 4.

Question: In Python, a module-level `client = ApiClient()` is created at import. Tests and apps fight over it. What is the issue?
Option A: Imports cannot run constructors.
Option B: Import-time globals are a hidden singleton: hard to fake, created even if unused, and shared across tests.
Option C: Module-level objects are recreated on every function call.
Option D: CPython isolates module globals per request.

Question: In Python, why can `list.append` in a loop be fine, but repeated `list = list + [x]` be quadratic?
Option A: append reallocates exponentially (amortized O(1)); concatenating two lists copies on every step.
Option B: append copies the whole list; `+` mutates in place.
Option C: Both are O(1); the quadratic story is a myth.
Option D: `+` uses C speed and is always faster than append.

Question: In Python, why does `if user_ids:` treat an empty list as false, and why is that a trap when `user_ids` can also be `None`?
Option A: Empty list and None are the same object, so you cannot distinguish them.
Option B: Both are falsy, so you cannot tell 'no rows' from 'caller forgot to pass the list' unless you check `is None` first.
Option C: Empty lists are truthy in CPython; only None is falsy.
Option D: `if user_ids` always copies the list, so None would throw before the test.

Question: In Python, why is `datetime.now()` without a timezone a production footgun?
Option A: Naive datetimes cannot be stored.
Option B: They look like timestamps but do not know their zone; DST and UTC conversion will silently be wrong.
Option C: now() always returns UTC.
Option D: Python forbids naive datetimes in 3.x.

Question: In Python, you catch `except Exception` around a web handler and return 200. What did you hide?
Option A: Nothing; Exception does not include programming errors.
Option B: Almost every failure, including bugs you needed to see; the client thinks success while you swallowed the traceback.
Option C: Only network errors; SyntaxError still propagates.
Option D: Exception is BaseException, so you also catch KeyboardInterrupt on purpose.

Question: In Python, you iterate a dict and delete keys as you go (`for k in d: del d[k]`). What happens?
Option A: CPython always allows mutating the dict while iterating.
Option B: RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration — iterate on `list(d)` if you must delete.
Option C: Deleted keys are skipped silently and the loop finishes.
Option D: The dict freezes a snapshot, so deletes never affect the loop.

Question: You spawn 8 threads to crunch CPU-bound numpy-free Python loops on an 8-core machine. Why don't you get 8× speedup?
Option A: The GIL allows only one thread at a time to execute bytecode, so CPU-bound threads take turns.

Question: In Redis Cluster, a key maps to a hash slot. Multi-key commands work only when:

Question: In Redis, KEYS * in production is dangerous because:

Option C: It evicts all keys
Option D: It only works in Cluster

Question: In Redis, RDB snapshots vs AOF: you need to lose at most a few milliseconds of writes on crash. Which direction is right?
Option A: RDB every hour is enough because snapshots are always up to the last command.
Option B: AOF with frequent fsync (or hybrid) replays recent writes; RDB-only can lose everything since the last snapshot.
Option C: Neither persists; Redis is memory-only by design and cannot survive a process crash.
Option D: RDB is always more durable than AOF because it is binary.

Question: In Redis, RDB vs AOF in one line:
Option A: RDB is a point-in-time snapshot; AOF logs writes for a tighter durability window, at more I/O cost
Option B: AOF is only for cluster slots
Option C: RDB and AOF are identical
Option D: RDB makes Redis multi-threaded

Question: In Redis, TTL on a cache key means:

Option B: Redis may drop the key after expiry; the source of truth must still exist elsewhere if you need it
Option C: The key is persisted to RDB immediately
Option D: Replicas cannot read it

Question: In Redis, a cache stampede (thundering herd) is:
Option A: AOF rewrite using too many cores
Option B: Many clients missing the same expired key at once and all hitting the database together
Option C: Cluster slot migration
Option D: Replica promotion

Question: In Redis, a huge value on one hot key is a problem even with Cluster because:
Option A: Slots cannot hold strings
Option B: That key still lives on one node and is served by one command loop; Cluster shards keys, not a single giant value
Option C: RDB cannot snapshot large keys
Option D: TTL cannot apply

Question: In Redis, cache stampede: a hot key expires and 2,000 app servers miss at once. What is the real failure mode?
Option A: Redis refuses the first GET after expiry.
Option B: They all stampede the origin (DB) together; Redis itself is usually fine, the database is not.
Option C: AOF rewrite blocks until every server has the new value.

Question: In Redis, if the process restarts and you only have occasional RDB snapshots, you should expect:

Option B: Loss of writes since the last snapshot unless AOF (or a real database) covers them

Question: In Redis, maxmemory is hit and the policy is allkeys-lru. What happens to a new SET?
Option A: Redis refuses all commands forever

Option D: Redis converts to AOF-only

Question: In Redis, noeviction as a maxmemory policy means:

Option C: Redis becomes the source of truth

Question: In Redis, pipelining helps throughput because:

Option A: Runs on extra cores automatically

Option A: Other clients keep getting p95 latency because Redis pipelines around the slow command.
